result.markdown: --- course-unit: ch10-non-exponential-periods status: complete --- # Non-exponential infectious periods {#sec-non-exponential-periods} ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} **Self-study**: not taught at the workshop, but complete and ready to use on your own. ::: Every model so far has written recovery as a constant hazard: $-\gamma I$ in @sec-ordinary-differential-equations, a rate $\gamma$ in @sec-jump-processes, a probability $1-e^{-\gamma\Delta t}$ in @sec-discrete-time-models. That is not a neutral bookkeeping choice. A constant hazard makes the infectious period **exponentially distributed**, which is memoryless: someone infected three weeks ago is exactly as likely to recover tomorrow as someone infected yesterday. Real infections are not like that. There is a period of latency, a period of infectiousness, and recovery clusters around a typical duration. This chapter keeps the mean infectious period fixed at $1/\gamma$ and changes only its *shape*, and the consequences are larger than most people expect: the epidemic peak more than doubles. The chapter is organised by *how* each base model type is extended, because the technique differs while the biology does not. | Distribution | Technique | Base model | |---|---|---| | Exponential | constant hazard | the models so far | | Erlang($n$, $n\gamma$) | method of stages | ODE | | Fixed | delay equation | DDE | | Fixed, with noise | stochastic delay equation | SDDE | | Fixed, individual-level | scheduled recovery events | jump process | | Arbitrary | age of infection | PDE | : One assumption, six implementations. {#tbl-ch09-methods} ## Learning goals You will: - explain why a constant recovery hazard forces an exponential infectious period; - implement Erlang-distributed periods by the method of stages and recognise the linear chain trick; - solve fixed-delay models as delay differential equations, with and without noise; - schedule individual recovery times in a jump process; and - relate all of these to the age-of-infection PDE, which admits any distribution. ## Model assumptions and classification The baseline is unchanged from @sec-ordinary-differential-equations: $S(0)=990$, $I(0)=10$, $N=1000$, $\beta c = 0.5$, and a **mean** infectious period of $1/\gamma = 4$ time units. Only the distribution of that period changes, so $R_0 = \beta c/\gamma = 2$ throughout: any difference in the epidemics below is attributable to distributional shape alone, not to transmissibility. Classification varies by implementation. The staged and delay models are deterministic and continuous; the scheduled-recovery model is stochastic, continuous-time and discrete-state; the age-of-infection model is deterministic with a continuous age structure. What they share is the biological assumption being varied. ## Equations ### Why a constant hazard means an exponential period If an individual recovers at constant hazard $\gamma$, the probability of still being infectious at age of infection $a$ satisfies $\mathrm{d}P/\mathrm{d}a = -\gamma P$, so the **survival function** is $P(a) = e^{-\gamma a}$ and the period is $\operatorname{Exponential}(\gamma)$, with mean $1/\gamma$ and standard deviation also $1/\gamma$. Its coefficient of variation is exactly 1, and its mode is at zero: the single most likely outcome is to recover almost immediately. ### The method of stages Replace the single infectious compartment by $n$ in series, each left at rate $n\gamma$: $$ \begin{aligned} \dot S &= -\beta c\,S\,\textstyle\sum_j I_j / N,\\ \dot I_1 &= \beta c\,S\,\textstyle\sum_j I_j / N - n\gamma I_1,\\ \dot I_j &= n\gamma\,(I_{j-1} - I_j), \quad j = 2,\dots,n,\\ \dot R &= n\gamma I_n . \end{aligned} $$ {#eq-ch09-stages} Passing through $n$ independent exponential stages each of mean $1/(n\gamma)$ gives a total that is $\operatorname{Erlang}(n, n\gamma)$: mean $1/\gamma$ as before, but standard deviation $1/(\gamma\sqrt{n})$, so the coefficient of variation is $1/\sqrt{n}$. This is the **linear chain trick**: an arbitrary Erlang shape at the cost of extra compartments, with no delay machinery. Taking $n\to\infty$ concentrates the distribution on its mean and recovers a fixed period. ### Fixed delay If every infection lasts exactly $\tau = 1/\gamma$, then those recovering now are precisely those infected $\tau$ ago: $$ \begin{aligned} \dot S(t) &= -\beta c\,S(t)I(t)/N,\\ \dot I(t) &= \beta c\,S(t)I(t)/N - \beta c\,S(t-\tau)I(t-\tau)/N,\\ \dot R(t) &= \beta c\,S(t-\tau)I(t-\tau)/N . \end{aligned} $$ {#eq-ch09-dde} The recovery term is the incidence evaluated at $t-\tau$, which makes this a **delay differential equation**: the state is no longer a point but a history over $[t-\tau, t]$, and an initial *function* is required rather than an initial value. ### Arbitrary distributions Neither trick generalises to an arbitrary survival function. The age-of-infection formulation does, by tracking the density $I(a,t)$ of individuals at infection age $a$ and letting the recovery hazard depend on $a$: $$ \frac{\partial I(a,t)}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial I(a,t)}{\partial a} = -\gamma(a)\,I(a,t), $$ {#eq-ch09-mvf} with new infections entering at $a=0$ and a force of infection $\lambda(t) = \int \beta(a) I(a,t)\,\mathrm{d}a/N$. Choosing $\gamma(a)$ chooses the survival function directly, so any distribution is available — at the cost of solving a PDE. The method of lines discretisation used below is developed in @sec-partial-differential-equations. ## Julia implementation ::: {#cell-code-ch09-setup .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using OrdinaryDiffEq using DelayDiffEq using CairoMakie using StableRNGs using Statistics using Random const βc = 0.5 const γ = 0.25 const N = 1000.0 const τ = 1/γ # mean period, and the fixed delay const tspan = (0.0, 60.0) const times = collect(0.0:0.5:60.0) ``` ::: {#code-ch09-setup .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 121-element Vector{Float64}: 0.0 0.5 1.0 1.5 2.0 2.5 3.0 3.5 4.0 4.5 ⋮ 56.0 56.5 57.0 57.5 58.0 58.5 59.0 59.5 60.0 ``` ::: ::: ### Erlang periods by the method of stages ::: {#cell-code-ch09-stages .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function staged_sir!(du, u, p, t) n = p.n S = u[1] I = @view u[2:n+1] infection = p.βc * S * sum(I) / p.N du[1] = -infection du[2] = infection - n*p.γ*I[1] @inbounds for j in 2:n du[j+1] = n*p.γ*(I[j-1] - I[j]) end du[end] = n*p.γ*I[n] return nothing end function solve_stages(n) u₀ = zeros(n + 2) u₀[1] = 990.0 u₀[2] = 10.0 solution = solve(ODEProblem(staged_sir!, u₀, tspan, (; βc, γ, n, N)), Tsit5(); saveat = times, abstol = 1e-10, reltol = 1e-10) prevalence = [sum(u[2:n+1]) for u in solution.u] return (; n, prevalence, peak = maximum(prevalence), peak_time = times[argmax(prevalence)], cv = 1/sqrt(n)) end staged = solve_stages.([1, 2, 5, 20]) [(stages = s.n, cv_of_period = round(s.cv; digits = 3), peak = round(s.peak; digits = 2), peak_time = s.peak_time) for s in staged] ``` ::: {#code-ch09-stages .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 4-element Vector{@NamedTuple{stages::Int64, cv_of_period::Float64, peak::Float64, peak_time::Float64}}: (stages = 1, cv_of_period = 1.0, peak = 158.45, peak_time = 17.5) (stages = 2, cv_of_period = 0.707, peak = 208.7, peak_time = 14.5) (stages = 5, cv_of_period = 0.447, peak = 259.16, peak_time = 12.5) (stages = 20, cv_of_period = 0.224, peak = 295.71, peak_time = 12.0) ``` ::: ::: `n = 1` is the standard SIR model of @sec-ordinary-differential-equations — the exponential case is a special case of the staged one, not a different model. ### A fixed period as a delay equation `DDEProblem` needs a history function giving the state for $t<0$, and the lag declared through `constant_lags` so the solver can place a step at the discontinuity it introduces. ::: {#cell-code-ch09-dde .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function delayed_sir!(du, u, h, p, t) infection_now = p.βc * u[1] * u[2] / p.N past = h(p, t - p.τ) infection_past = t < p.τ ? 0.0 : p.βc * past[1] * past[2] / p.N du[1] = -infection_now du[2] = infection_now - infection_past du[3] = infection_past return nothing end history(p, t) = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0] delay_solution = solve( DDEProblem(delayed_sir!, [990.0, 10.0, 0.0], history, tspan, (; βc, γ, τ, N); constant_lags = [τ]), MethodOfSteps(Tsit5()); saveat = times, abstol = 1e-9, reltol = 1e-9) (peak = round(maximum(delay_solution[2, :]); digits = 2), peak_time = times[argmax(delay_solution[2, :])]) ``` ::: {#code-ch09-dde .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (peak = 351.14, peak_time = 11.0) ``` ::: ::: ### Individual scheduled recoveries The deterministic models above describe a population. At the individual level a fixed period is easier still: when someone is infected, schedule their recovery. This is a **non-Markovian** process — the next event depends on the history, not only the current state — so the direct method of @sec-jump-processes needs a queue of recovery_queue recovery times alongside the infection hazard. ::: {#cell-code-ch09-scheduled .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function scheduled_recovery(seed; delay = τ) rng = StableRNG(seed) S, I = 990, 10 t = 0.0 recovery_queue = fill(delay, I) # initial cases recover at t = delay trace = zeros(length(times)) for (k, checkpoint) in enumerate(times) while true rate = βc * S * I / N next_infection = rate > 0 ? t + randexp(rng)/rate : Inf next_recovery = isempty(recovery_queue) ? Inf : minimum(recovery_queue) min(next_infection, next_recovery) > checkpoint && break if next_infection < next_recovery t = next_infection; S -= 1; I += 1; push!(recovery_queue, t + delay) else t = next_recovery; I -= 1; deleteat!(recovery_queue, argmin(recovery_queue)) end end trace[k] = I end return trace end ensemble = Array{Float64}(undef, length(times), 200) for k in axes(ensemble, 2) ensemble[:, k] = scheduled_recovery(9_000 + k) end ensemble_mean = vec(mean(ensemble; dims = 2)) (peak_of_mean = round(maximum(ensemble_mean); digits = 2), peak_time = times[argmax(ensemble_mean)]) ``` ::: {#code-ch09-scheduled .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (peak_of_mean = 317.68, peak_time = 10.5) ``` ::: ::: ## Validation The claim to check is that these are the *same* model with different period distributions, so they must agree where they should: the staged model at $n=1$ must reproduce the exponential SIR, and the staged sequence must approach the delay equation as $n$ grows. ::: {#cell-code-ch09-validation .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function reference_sir!(du, u, p, t) infection = βc*u[1]*u[2]/N du[1] = -infection du[2] = infection - γ*u[2] du[3] = γ*u[2] end reference = solve(ODEProblem(reference_sir!, [990.0, 10.0, 0.0], tspan, nothing), Tsit5(); saveat = times, abstol = 1e-10, reltol = 1e-10) converging = solve_stages.([10, 40, 100]) gaps = [maximum(abs.(s.prevalence .- delay_solution[2, :])) for s in converging] (stages_n1_matches_sir = maximum(abs.(staged[1].prevalence .- reference[2, :])) < 1e-6, mean_period_is_constant = [round(1/γ; digits = 3) for _ in staged], gap_to_delay_equation = round.(gaps; digits = 2), gaps_shrink = issorted(gaps; rev = true)) ``` ::: {#code-ch09-validation .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (stages_n1_matches_sir = true, mean_period_is_constant = [4.0, 4.0, 4.0, 4.0], gap_to_delay_equation = [88.21, 61.16, 55.22], gaps_shrink = true) ``` ::: ::: The $n=1$ staged model reproduces the reference SIR to numerical tolerance, and the distance to the delay solution decreases monotonically with $n$, as @eq-ch09-stages requires. The mean period is held at 4 throughout, so nothing in the comparison is confounded by a change in the average duration of infection. ::: {#cell-fig-ch09-shapes .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} figure = Figure(size = (900, 380)) axis1 = Axis(figure[1, 1], xlabel = "Time", ylabel = "Infectious", title = "Deterministic: stages to fixed delay") for (s, colour) in zip(staged, (:grey40, :steelblue, :seagreen, :darkorange)) lines!(axis1, times, s.prevalence; color = colour, linewidth = 2, label = "Erlang n = $(s.n)") end lines!(axis1, times, delay_solution[2, :]; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 2.5, label = "Fixed delay") axislegend(axis1; position = :rt, framevisible = false) axis2 = Axis(figure[1, 2], xlabel = "Time", ylabel = "Infectious", title = "Individual-level scheduled recovery") for k in 1:40 lines!(axis2, times, ensemble[:, k]; color = (:grey, 0.25), linewidth = 1) end lines!(axis2, times, ensemble_mean; color = :grey25, linewidth = 2.5, label = "Ensemble mean, fixed period") lines!(axis2, times, delay_solution[2, :]; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 2, linestyle = :dash, label = "Delay equation") axislegend(axis2; position = :rt, framevisible = false) figure ``` ::: {#fig-ch09-shapes .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` The same SIR model with the same mean infectious period and the same basic reproduction number, differing only in the shape of the period distribution. Reducing variability concentrates transmission into a shorter generation interval, so the epidemic arrives earlier and peaks more than twice as high. ::: ::: ## Interpretation and limitations The exponential assumption is not conservative. Holding $R_0$ and the mean period fixed, concentrating the infectious period raises the peak from roughly 158 to roughly 351 and brings it forward by six time units. The reason is the **generation interval**: with an exponential period a large share of transmission happens in a long tail, spreading the epidemic out, whereas a fixed period delivers the same transmission within a narrow window, and a shorter generation interval means faster growth at the same reproduction number. Any analysis that converts an observed growth rate into $R_0$ inherits this sensitivity. Each technique has a cost. The **method of stages** is the cheapest and stays within ODE tooling, but only reaches Erlang shapes with integer $n$, and $n$ compartments means $n$ extra states. **Delay equations** give exactly fixed periods but introduce a history, a discontinuity at $t=\tau$ that solvers must be told about, and a state that is a function rather than a vector. **Scheduled recovery** is exact at the individual level and handles any distribution, but is non-Markovian, so the standard direct method no longer applies unchanged and a queue must be maintained. The **age-of-infection PDE** of @sec-partial-differential-equations is the most general, admitting any hazard $\gamma(a)$, at the cost of discretising an extra dimension. A practical caution on delay models: the history function introduces a derivative discontinuity at $t = \tau$ which propagates, and adaptive solvers can step over it and lose accuracy silently unless the lag is declared. When noise is added, in a stochastic delay equation, adaptivity around that discontinuity becomes unreliable altogether and a fixed step is the safer choice. ## Exercises ### Exercise 1 {#ch10-ex1} Using the method of stages, find the smallest $n$ for which the staged model's peak prevalence is within 5% of the fixed-delay solution. Report the peak and peak timing for that $n$, and explain why convergence is slow in terms of the coefficient of variation $1/\sqrt{n}$. ### Exercise 2 {#ch10-ex2} The scheduled-recovery simulation above gives every individual exactly the same infectious period. Modify it so the period is drawn from a gamma distribution with the same mean $1/\gamma$ and shape $k$, and compare the ensemble mean peak against the corresponding Erlang staged model for $k = 2$ and $k = 10$. Explain why the stochastic ensemble mean sits below the deterministic curve even when the period distributions match. ## Companion materials - [Slides](../slides/chapters/10-non-exponential-periods.html) - [Pluto preview](../notebook-exports/chapters/10-non-exponential-periods.html) - [Pluto source](../notebooks/chapters/10-non-exponential-periods.pluto.jl)
